ety.text: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.

senses.d: To take voluntarily (a child of other parents) to be in the place of, or as, one's own child.
ex: A friend of mine recently adopted a Chinese baby girl found on the streets of Beijing.

senses.d: To obtain (a pet) from a shelter or the wild.
ex: We're going to adopt a Dalmatian.

senses.d: To contribute towards the upkeep of (a child or animal), in exchange for occasional stories, pictures, etc.
ex: We adopted an elephant at the local zoo.

senses.d: To take by choice into the scope of one's responsibility.
ex: This supermarket chain adopts several families every Yuletide, providing them with money and groceries for the holidays.

senses.d: To take or receive as one's own what is not so naturally.
ex: He adopted a new look in order to fit in with his new workmates.

senses.d: To select and take or approve.
ex: to adopt the view or policy of another
These are resolutions that were adopted.

senses.d: To beat an opponent ten times in a row.
ex: The match was not even close; the IM made amateurish blunders and ended up getting adopted.

ety.text: First attested ?1440, from Middle English adolescent, from Middle French adolescent or directly from Latin adolescentem, accusative form of adolescens, present participle of adolēscere (“to become adult, grow up”), from ad- (“to”) + alēscere (“to grow or become nourished”). The adjective first appeared in 1785.

senses.d: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.
ex: Schools, unless discipline were doubly strong, / Detain their adolescent charge too long.

senses.d: A person who is in adolescence; someone who has reached puberty but is not yet an adult.
ex: It may be wartime, but Miss Adolescent wants her fun!
‘A healthy adolescent might be expected to produce five hundred billion blood cells a day.’
